1️⃣ Connect to edu/comparison websites where my competitors are already quoted, to see if they allow for sponsored placements.

Argument 1: Nearly 90% of third-party AI citations come from listicles, comparisons, and review sites, and 80% of cited brands sit in the first three positions on those pages.

Argument 2: 85% of brand mentions in AI search come from third-party sources, not the brand’s own domain.

2️⃣ Restructure content in my blogs/support pages so they include more lists and comparisons.

Argument: Lists and tables appear in nearly 80% of ChatGPT-cited pages, compared to 29% of Google's top organic results.

3️⃣ Optimize for the classic H1-to-H2-to-H3 heading hierarchy.

Argument: A clean H1-to-H2-to-H3 heading hierarchy increases citation odds by 2.8x in AI answers.

4️⃣ Add FAQs to your key pages.

Argument: Pages with FAQs are 40% more likely to be cited in AI answers.

5️⃣ Update pages that are already cited by AI at least once every three months so they don't lose their position.

Argument: Pages updated within three months are three times more likely to be cited in AI answers.

🗡️ What DeFi Shipped 🚢 (Oct 9):

Hyperliquid landed on the Bloomberg Terminal, USDT is launching on Bitcoin, and more.

10 updates worth catching up on:

• @HyperliquidX just landed on the Bloomberg Terminal, the default screen of TradFi. It's a massive legitimacy signal.

• @tether launches USDT on Bitcoin this month through RGB, with private transfers, direct BTC/USDT swaps, and BTC-collateralized lending.

• @aave proposed an Aave Foundation, a memberless Cayman Islands entity that would hold Aave's trademark and IP on behalf of the DAO.

• @Ostium is rebuilding as Gateway, a whitelisted API and liquidity layer selling RWA perps access to venues, family offices, and pro desks.

• @virtuals_io opened Virtuals App in closed beta: a personal AI with its own wallet and market access. You set its limits and permissions, then put it to work like your own quant.

• @DriftFDN opened DFX claims and redemptions for victims of its April 1 exploit, paying 1 DFX per $1 lost. DFX currently redeems for about $0.01 each.

• Chromia is proposing to remove its 978M CHR supply cap and issue 125,000 new CHR daily. That's ~45.6M CHR a year, or ~4.7% inflation in year one.

• @longdotxyz rolled out a community vault LP upgrade that moves stock-pair vault liquidity into USDG/STOCK pools on Robinhood Chain. The goal is to make LONG pairs the largest external LPs for tokenized stocks, with LP fees compounding back into the vault.

• @theInterfold shipped receipt-free secret ballots on Ethereum mainnet. Ballots stay private, the tally is encrypted, and threshold decryption produces a verifiable result with no trusted hardware.

My favorite update this week is Hyperliquid landing on Bloomberg.

Bloomberg now streams Hyperliquid perps on the S&P 500, gold, and crude. 

When Wall Street shuts down on Friday afternoon and something big happens over the weekend, traders on the terminal can still see where the market is pricing it, live and onchain.

For years TradFi rolled its eyes at crypto. Now it's checking Hyperliquid on a Saturday to see where oil is trading.

It’s a fair point regarding bragging, but I believe bragging serves a purpose.

In our business, people like Michael Burry and countless others on X write intelligently and eloquently, attracting tens or even hundreds of thousands of followers. Yet you often have no idea what their actual track records look like or how good they really are.

I suspect that if many of these people published their returns over the past ten years, they would have significantly underperformed the market, and far fewer people would follow them.

People publish convincing ideas, and readers simply assume they know what they’re doing. But writing intelligently and making money in the market are two very different skills.

Since people often find it difficult to believe that valuable information can be free, I occasionally share my returns to demonstrate that my ideas actually generate alpha. They’re not just clever theories I throw into the ether.

Those posts also attract more people to my account, which helps my ideas reach a wider audience.

I don’t want anyone to follow me blindly. Quite the opposite. I want people to see the results, become curious, investigate my ideas, and do their own research.

Ultimately, I’m trying to bring a little more transparency and integrity to a space where eloquent writing is too often mistaken for investment skill.

Ideas are easy to publish. Generating alpha consistently is a different story.

Hey mate, the largest account I manage is my own, and I’m much more active in it.

I don’t manage all accounts the same way. Sometimes I point out that the accounts I trade less actively actually perform better, while at other times, the more actively managed accounts outperform.

I also take significantly more risk in my personal account than I do in my clients’ accounts. For example, I would never allocate 49% to $SNAP, 50% to $ZIM, or 40% to $WGS in a client account.

I hope this clarifies things.

It’s a fair point regarding bragging, but I believe bragging serves a purpose.

In our business, people like Michael Burry and countless others on X write intelligently and eloquently, attracting tens or even hundreds of thousands of followers. Yet you often have no idea what their actual track records look like or how good they really are.

I suspect that if many of these people published their returns over the past ten years, they would have significantly underperformed the market, and far fewer people would follow them.

People publish convincing ideas, and readers simply assume they know what they’re doing. But writing intelligently and making money in the market are two very different skills.

Since people often find it difficult to believe that valuable information can be free, I occasionally share my returns to demonstrate that my ideas actually generate alpha. They’re not just clever theories I throw into the ether.

Those posts also attract more people to my account, which helps my ideas reach a wider audience.

I don’t want anyone to follow me blindly. Quite the opposite. I want people to see the results, become curious, investigate my ideas, and do their own research.

Ultimately, I’m trying to bring a little more transparency and integrity to a space where eloquent writing is too often mistaken for investment skill.

Ideas are easy to publish. Generating alpha consistently is a different story.

My thesis on $UBER is relatively simple.

David Tepper of Appaloosa Management and Bill Ackman of Pershing Square have done their homework before they put it as such a big allocation. I assume they’ve done extensive research and concluded that Uber is unlikely to be significantly disrupted by autonomous vehicles and AI.

And I can buy the stock at a 10–20% discount to what they paid.

So far, the disruption hasn’t materialized in a meaningful way. However, this approach to investing, relying partly on the research and conviction of highly successful investors, hasn’t worked particularly well for me so far.

I increased my position again after $UBER broke back above $70, having been stuck below that level for a while. I saw the breakout as a positive signal and decided to add.

In the grand scheme of things, I’m roughly flat or sitting on a small loss on $UBER.

Let’s see how it plays out.

tweets.text:
Falling token prices + sticky-high GPU prices is classic Jevons paradox playing out in real time.

Inference is getting dramatically cheaper (efficiency, competition, Blackwell-scale gains). That doesn’t reduce compute demand - it explodes it. Cheaper tokens unlock agentic workflows, more coding, more automation and more users. Total token volume is growing far faster than unit costs are falling, so the scarce resource (GPUs, HBM, power, data centres) stays tight.

Implications for AI infrastructure stocks:

- GPU / accelerator makers (NVDA and peers) still benefit. High utilisation + sustained scarcity supports pricing and volume.
- Memory (HBM/GDDR), networking and power infrastructure see durable demand as inference scales.
- Hyperscalers and neoclouds face a margin squeeze if token price declines outrun volume growth, but capacity constraints and rising absolute spend so far argue demand is still winning.
- The shift to inference-heavy workloads favours specialised silicon and high-throughput systems over pure training clusters.

Bottom line: AI is proliferating faster than efficiency is reducing the need for hardware. Unit prices collapse, total spend and infrastructure demand keep rising. That’s bullish for the physical layer as long as volume growth remains the dominant force. https://t.co/YKr5pL78cE
